crime_highlights: Mr. Goodacre was wearing a mask
He broke the driver's door window by striking it with an object
That object struck Ms. Tatla and broke her nose
He opened the door from the inside, told her to get out of the car, and he drove away
Ms. Tatla said that she remains fearful even two years after the offence
she is terrified of waiting in her car
rationale_highlights: I return to the importance and significance in this case of adhering to the spirit and legal principles from Gladue and Ipeelee

Mr. Goodacre's circumstances are an illustration of how the historical mistreatment of Canada's Aboriginal peoples filters down to continue to negatively impact individuals, sadly leading them into the criminal justice system
the proposed sentence is one that best fulfils my obligation to sentence you while taking into account your status as an Aboriginal offender

crime_highlights: Stephen served a crucial role in the plot by driving the vehicle in which the victim was kept for some time
he did hit the victim at least once

rationale_highlights: He avoided joining any Metis groups when he was younger for fear of being subjected to racism
there is no onus on an offender to prove a direct connection between their Aboriginal heritage and the index offence
I accept that the Gladue Report still supports a more controlled sentence
note: Crime passage lacks victim harm; the court states weak, muted effect of Metis heritage.

crime_highlights: This conduct continued until R.M. was 14 years old, in 2015

B.D.M. took his granddaughters and his young son on vacation to Cache Creek
rationale_highlights: His father was of Métis heritage, which triggers the application of the Gladue factor in sentencing
an atrocious upbringing filled with violence, abuse, and neglect
